title: Tenants
description: Is any Kubeletto tenant misbehaving or costing the platform? Namespace and pod counts, cold-start churn, crash loops, throttled logs, the network fence and the worker's inbound traffic, and which tenants send, receive and use the most (network, CPU and memory from the kubelet's cAdvisor). Open it after K8sTenant* or TenantWorkerInboundSustained, and on the weekly tenant review. Tenants are opaque ids (kl-<id>-<id>), so the per-tenant views are top-10 tables. Per-tenant request counts are not in Prometheus.

panels.title: Is a tenant misbehaving or costing the platform?
Worker inbound, 30 min
panels.description: Bit rate received on the Kubeletto tenant worker's eth0, as a 30-minute average (rule TenantWorkerInboundSustained: above 2.5 Mbit/s for 2 hours, about 27 GB a day). Red means a tenant pod is pulling from the internet or the worker is busy inside the lab: eth0 also carries the cluster's own traffic. Next: the network row below, then services/kubeletto/tenant-bandwidth.sh to name the tenant.

panels.title: Tenants over the churn line
panels.description: Tenant namespaces that started more than 200 distinct pods in 24 hours (rule K8sTenantColdStartChurn, severity info, 1 hour). A scale-to-zero app that something pings every couple of minutes starts a fresh pod each time. Orange, not red: it is for the weekly review, and most of these cost CPU, not bandwidth. The table below names them.

panels.title: Crash-looping tenants
panels.description: Tenant namespaces whose app container restarted more than 10 times in the last hour, summed over the namespace's pods (rule K8sTenantContainerRestarting: 3 hours running). A crash loop, not a deploy; the usual cause is a required secret that the owner never set. The owner's to fix: tell them what the log says.

panels.title: Namespaces without the fence
panels.description: Tenant namespaces with no kubeletto-base-policy (rule K8sTenantNamespaceWithoutNetworkPolicy, critical, 15 minutes). That policy keeps tenant pods off the lab network and the shared Postgres and Valkey, so a namespace without it is an isolation hole. A namespace seconds old is normal.

targets.expr: count((kube_namespace_created{job="service_dmz", namespace=~"kl-.*"} unless on (namespace) kube_networkpolicy_created{job="service_dmz", networkpolicy="kubeletto-base-policy"}) and on () (count(kube_networkpolicy_created{job="service_dmz"}) > 0))

panels.title: Log events throttled, 15 min
panels.description: Log events Vector's per-tenant cap dropped in the last 15 minutes (rule K8sTenantLogsThrottled: any drop). The tenant's `kubeletto logs` has holes for that window; its app is unaffected. Reads 0 while no drop has ever happened: the counter does not exist until the first one, so 0 here is also what an absent series looks like (the Logs row shows whether Vector is scraped at all).

panels.title: Pods unschedulable
panels.description: Pods the scheduler refused, cluster-wide (rule K8sPodUnschedulable: 5 minutes). When it is a tenant's pod, that tenant cannot start; the usual cause is memory requests above what the worker can hand out (K8sNodeMemoryRequestsHigh). A brief Pending during a cold start is normal and is not counted here.

panels.title: Tenant inbound, total
panels.description: Bit rate received by all tenant pods together (kl-*), summed over their eth0 as the kubelet's cAdvisor counts it, with the trend behind the number. It is what the tenants' apps take in, from customers and from the internet; the 'Worker inbound, 30 min' tile is the whole node's eth0 and the one the alert watches. No alert rule: a context number. These series exist since 2026-11-09, and a pod's first seconds are not counted, so a tenant that is mostly cold starts reads low. The tenant namespace count is on the fence row.

panels.title: Tenant pods running
panels.description: Tenant pods in phase Running right now (one pod holds the app and its queue-proxy sidecar). Scale-to-zero makes it swing by a few every minute. No alert rule: a context number.

panels.title: Who is using the line? (the worker's network)
k3s-worker network (TenantWorkerInboundSustained)
panels.description: Bit rate on the worker's eth0, where every tenant pod runs (rule TenantWorkerInboundSustained: the 30-minute average above the dashed 2.5 Mbit/s for 2 hours). The WAN's inbound is nearly all this node, so a flat high inbound line is the pattern of 2026-11-06, when one free app woken every 2 minutes pulled 40 to 50 GB a day from the internet. eth0 also carries lab-internal traffic, so it can read above the WAN.

panels.title: Worker inbound against what customers send in
panels.description: The worker's inbound next to the bytes customers upload through the public edge (Traefik request bodies) and the router's WAN inbound. The gap between the worker line and the Traefik line is what the worker receives besides customers' uploads: image pulls, what tenant apps fetch from the internet and the platform's own pods (the next panel shows how much of it tenant pods account for). At the time of writing customers' uploads are a rounding error against the worker's several Mbit/s, which is why the hog is a pod pulling data, not traffic to it.

panels.title: Worker inbound: tenant pods against the whole node
panels.description: The worker's inbound bit rate from three angles: the node's own eth0 as the kubelet counts it (the series with no namespace and no pod), the same interface from node_exporter (a cross-check: over 15 minutes they agree within a few percent, a wider gap means one source is stale) and the sum of all tenant pods. 'Node minus tenant pods' (kubelet node line minus tenants) is how much of the line tenants do not account for: platform pods on the worker, image pulls and other host traffic. Read it as an estimate, not an exact subtraction: a pod's counter also holds traffic that never leaves the node (the local DNS), and the node's counter holds the overlay's headers. A tenant line close to the node line would point at the tenants; a tenant line far below it means most of the node's traffic is not tenant pods. The series exist since 2026-11-09: wait for an hour of history before reading a pattern. Outbound is in the tables below.

targets.expr: sum(rate(container_network_receive_bytes_total{job="service_dmz", port="30599", instance="k3s-worker", namespace="", pod=""}[$__rate_interval])) * 8 - sum (rate(container_network_receive_bytes_total{job="service_dmz", port="30599", namespace=~"kl-.*", pod!="", instance="k3s-worker"}[$__rate_interval])) * 8

panels.title: Which tenants send and receive the most? (network, bit/s)
Top 10 tenants by inbound network
panels.description: The 10 tenant namespaces that received the most bits per second over the last 5 minutes, with their 15-minute average and their share of all tenants' inbound. Inbound is what the tenant's pods take in: customers' requests and whatever the app downloads. Read it next to the worker panel above: the tenants are one part of the node's line. A tenant near the top for a long time, with a high share, is the one to look at (services/kubeletto/tenant-bandwidth.sh names the slug). The series exist since 2026-11-09 and a pod's first seconds are not counted, so a tenant that is mostly cold starts is read low. A literal 5 and 15 minute window, not the dashboard range.

targets.expr: topk(10, sum by (namespace) (rate(container_network_receive_bytes_total{job="service_dmz", port="30599", namespace=~"kl-.*", pod!=""}[5m])) * 8)

(sum by (namespace) (rate(container_network_receive_bytes_total{job="service_dmz", port="30599", namespace=~"kl-.*", pod!=""}[15m])) * 8) and on (namespace) topk(10, sum by (namespace) (rate(container_network_receive_bytes_total{job="service_dmz", port="30599", namespace=~"kl-.*", pod!=""}[5m])) * 8)

(sum by (namespace) (rate(container_network_receive_bytes_total{job="service_dmz", port="30599", namespace=~"kl-.*", pod!=""}[5m])) * 8) / scalar(sum (rate(container_network_receive_bytes_total{job="service_dmz", port="30599", namespace=~"kl-.*", pod!=""}[5m])) * 8) and on (namespace) topk(10, sum by (namespace) (rate(container_network_receive_bytes_total{job="service_dmz", port="30599", namespace=~"kl-.*", pod!=""}[5m])) * 8)

panels.title: Top 10 tenants by outbound network
panels.description: The 10 tenant namespaces that sent the most bits per second over the last 5 minutes, with their 15-minute average and their share of all tenants' outbound: responses to customers and whatever the app uploads. The same reading as the inbound table; a tenant high in both is busy, high only in outbound is serving content. The series exist since 2026-11-09. A literal 5 and 15 minute window, not the dashboard range.

targets.expr: topk(10, sum by (namespace) (rate(container_network_transmit_bytes_total{job="service_dmz", port="30599", namespace=~"kl-.*", pod!=""}[5m])) * 8)

(sum by (namespace) (rate(container_network_transmit_bytes_total{job="service_dmz", port="30599", namespace=~"kl-.*", pod!=""}[15m])) * 8) and on (namespace) topk(10, sum by (namespace) (rate(container_network_transmit_bytes_total{job="service_dmz", port="30599", namespace=~"kl-.*", pod!=""}[5m])) * 8)

(sum by (namespace) (rate(container_network_transmit_bytes_total{job="service_dmz", port="30599", namespace=~"kl-.*", pod!=""}[5m])) * 8) / scalar(sum (rate(container_network_transmit_bytes_total{job="service_dmz", port="30599", namespace=~"kl-.*", pod!=""}[5m])) * 8) and on (namespace) topk(10, sum by (namespace) (rate(container_network_transmit_bytes_total{job="service_dmz", port="30599", namespace=~"kl-.*", pod!=""}[5m])) * 8)

panels.title: Top 5 tenants by inbound, over time
panels.description: Inbound bit rate of the 5 tenants that rank highest at the right edge of the dashboard's range, one line per tenant namespace over the whole range (fixed set: a tenant that was busy earlier but is quiet now is not drawn, the table is for now). Spikes are a pod pulling data or a burst of traffic; a flat line is a steady consumer. Start with the legend's mean. The data starts at 2026-11-09, so a long range is mostly empty until the history grows.

targets.expr: (sum by (namespace) (rate(container_network_receive_bytes_total{job="service_dmz", port="30599", namespace=~"kl-.*", pod!=""}[$__rate_interval])) * 8) and on (namespace) topk(5, sum by (namespace) (rate(container_network_receive_bytes_total{job="service_dmz", port="30599", namespace=~"kl-.*", pod!=""}[$__rate_interval] @ end())))

panels.title: Which tenants use the most CPU and memory?
Top 10 tenants by CPU (cores)
panels.description: CPU time the 10 busiest tenant namespaces used per second (1.0 = one full core), as a 5-minute and a 15-minute average, with their share of all tenants' CPU. Includes both containers of every pod, the app and its queue-proxy. A scale-to-zero app woken every couple of minutes shows its cold starts here as CPU. A tenant sustained at a core or more is a runaway or a heavy app. The worker has 3.5 cores to hand out. A literal 5 and 15 minute window: the series exist since 2026-11-09.

targets.expr: topk(10, sum by (namespace) (rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{job="service_dmz", port="30599", namespace=~"kl-.*", pod!=""}[5m])))

(sum by (namespace) (rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{job="service_dmz", port="30599", namespace=~"kl-.*", pod!=""}[15m]))) and on (namespace) topk(10, sum by (namespace) (rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{job="service_dmz", port="30599", namespace=~"kl-.*", pod!=""}[5m])))

(sum by (namespace) (rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{job="service_dmz", port="30599", namespace=~"kl-.*", pod!=""}[5m]))) / scalar(sum(sum by (namespace) (rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{job="service_dmz", port="30599", namespace=~"kl-.*", pod!=""}[5m])))) and on (namespace) topk(10, sum by (namespace) (rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{job="service_dmz", port="30599", namespace=~"kl-.*", pod!=""}[5m])))

panels.title: Top 10 tenants by memory used and requested
panels.description: The 10 tenant namespaces with the largest memory working set right now (what the kernel cannot reclaim: the number the OOM killer and the kubelet's eviction act on), next to what their pods reserve by request and the ratio. The worker hands out about 3.6 GB; the node-level version of the request side is rule K8sNodeMemoryRequestsHigh (90 %). Requests are overcommitted by design, so a ratio above 100 % is normal for an app bursting past its small request; a tenant with a large working set and a small request is the one that squeezes the node first. A tenant that scales to zero uses and reserves nothing, so the table moves with the traffic. A blank Requested is a pod that kube-state-metrics no longer lists (it just scaled down) while the kubelet still reports its last memory.

targets.expr: topk(10, sum by (namespace) (container_memory_working_set_bytes{job="service_dmz", port="30599", namespace=~"kl-.*", pod!=""}))

(sum by (namespace) (kube_pod_container_resource_requests{job="service_dmz", namespace=~"kl-.*", resource="memory"} * on (namespace, pod, uid) group_left () (kube_pod_status_phase{job="service_dmz", phase=~"Pending|Running"} == 1))) and on (namespace) topk(10, sum by (namespace) (container_memory_working_set_bytes{job="service_dmz", port="30599", namespace=~"kl-.*", pod!=""}))

(sum by (namespace) (container_memory_working_set_bytes{job="service_dmz", port="30599", namespace=~"kl-.*", pod!=""})) / on (namespace) (sum by (namespace) (kube_pod_container_resource_requests{job="service_dmz", namespace=~"kl-.*", resource="memory"} * on (namespace, pod, uid) group_left () (kube_pod_status_phase{job="service_dmz", phase=~"Pending|Running"} == 1))) and on (namespace) topk(10, sum by (namespace) (container_memory_working_set_bytes{job="service_dmz", port="30599", namespace=~"kl-.*", pod!=""}))

panels.title: Top 10 tenants by pods in 24 h (K8sTenantColdStartChurn)
panels.description: Distinct pods each tenant namespace started in the last 24 hours, the 10 highest (rule K8sTenantColdStartChurn, severity info: orange above 200). 200 is a pod every 7 minutes; about 715 means a request every 2 minutes. The 8 digits after kl- are the tenant id prefix: services/kubeletto/weekly-review.sh maps them to a slug and plan. Next: the network and CPU tables above, for whether the churn costs bandwidth or CPU (TenantWorkerInboundSustained says so for the line).

panels.title: Tenant pods started per hour
panels.description: Distinct tenant pods created in the trailing hour (kube_pod_created of every pod that left a series). An indirect cost signal: a woken scale-to-zero app starts a pod every time, and each start makes the node pull or check the image. Image pulls are the node's own traffic, so they are in the worker's line and in no tenant's pod counters. At the time of writing it sits near 150 an hour: five tenants woken every 2 minutes (the churn table beside it names them). A pod that lived less than one scrape interval is missed.

targets.legendFormat: pods started in the trailing hour

panels.title: Tenant pods and awake tenants
panels.description: Tenant pods Running and Pending, and how many tenant namespaces hold any pod. Pending is normal for a few seconds at a cold start; a Pending line that stays above 0 is a tenant that cannot start (rule K8sPodUnschedulable counts the unschedulable ones). The gap between tenants-with-a-pod and the 250-odd tenant namespaces (the fence row counts them) is the scale-to-zero saving.

panels.title: Tenants whose app container restarted in 24 h
panels.description: Tenant namespaces whose app container (user-container) restarted at least once in 24 hours, with the restarts of the last hour. The rule (K8sTenantContainerRestarting) wants more than 10 an hour for 3 hours, shown red. Empty is the normal state; a pod that is replaced rather than restarted does not count. Next: kubectl -n <namespace> logs <pod> -c user-container --previous.

targets.expr: sum by (namespace) (increase(kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total{job="service_dmz", namespace=~"kl-.*", container="user-container"}[1h])) and on (namespace) (sum by (namespace) (increase(kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total{job="service_dmz", namespace=~"kl-.*", container="user-container"}[1d])) > 0)

panels.title: Worst tenant, restarts in the trailing hour
panels.description: Restarts of tenant app containers in the trailing hour: the worst single tenant and the total. The dashed line is the 10 an hour of rule K8sTenantContainerRestarting, which must hold for 3 hours before it fires. A line that sits at 0 is healthy. increase() extrapolates, so a single restart can read slightly above 1.

panels.title: Why containers waited or stopped, last 24 h
panels.description: Containers of tenant pods by the reason they waited (ContainerCreating is every cold start; CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff or CreateContainerConfigError is a tenant that cannot run) and by why their last run ended (OOMKilled is an app over its memory limit; Error is a non-zero exit). Over 24 hours, so a reason that appeared and cleared still shows. No alert watches tenant containers' waiting reasons: K8sPlatformPodWaiting skips the kl-* namespaces on purpose.

panels.title: Are tenant logs throttled or lost?
Throttled log events, per node (K8sTenantLogsThrottled)
panels.description: Log events Vector's per-tenant throttle dropped, per node, in a trailing 15 minutes (rule K8sTenantLogsThrottled: any drop). Empty is the normal state: the counter has no series until the first drop. The runbook says it carries a per-tenant key label that names the tenant; that label is unverified (it has never been born), so the legend shows it only if it exists. The cap is 6000 events per 10 s per tenant per node.

panels.title: Log events lost by failure (K8sLogsDropped)
panels.description: Events Vector lost because a sink or transform failed, not because a filter or the throttle chose to (rule K8sLogsDropped: intentional=false, any in 15 minutes), and Vector's component errors. Empty is the normal state. A line here means the VictoriaLogs sink rejected or timed out; the lost lines do not come back.

panels.title: Log events dropped on purpose, per filter
panels.description: Events per second the filters discard by design: build logs and probe noise. Healthy and steady; a throttle drop would appear here too, as kubeletto_throttle_runtime. It doubles as proof that Vector is alive and counting.

panels.title: Vector scrape (is the throttle counter visible?)
panels.description: Whether Prometheus can read Vector's own metrics on each K3s node (target port 30598). When it is DOWN, the throttle and loss panels above are blind, not clean (TargetDown fires for it after 5 minutes).

panels.title: Is every tenant fenced off from the lab network?
Tenant namespaces without kubeletto-base-policy
panels.description: Tenant namespaces that carry no kubeletto-base-policy (rule K8sTenantNamespaceWithoutNetworkPolicy: critical after 15 minutes). Empty is the goal. A namespace created seconds ago is normal; one older than 15 minutes means core's quota/policy reconciler did not run for it: re-apply the policy or pause that tenant (the operator decides, it is customer-facing).

targets.expr: ((kube_namespace_created{job="service_dmz", namespace=~"kl-.*"} unless on (namespace) kube_networkpolicy_created{job="service_dmz", networkpolicy="kubeletto-base-policy"}) and on () (count(kube_networkpolicy_created{job="service_dmz"}) > 0)) * 1000

panels.title: Namespaces with the policy against tenant namespaces
panels.description: Tenant namespaces that carry the base policy next to all tenant namespaces. The two lines should lie on top of each other; a gap that opens when a tenant is created and closes within minutes is the reconciler working, one that stays open is the alert. If kube-state-metrics stops exporting networkpolicies the lower line vanishes and the rule's guard keeps it quiet: look here.

panels.title: Requests, disk and I/O per tenant: not in Prometheus
panels.description: Reading guide.

options.content: Traefik reports one service for all tenant apps (`traefik-user-apps-...`), so this board can show **all tenants together** but not one tenant. The per-tenant request count is Kubeletto's `usage_samples` (metric `http_requests`, 5-minute windows) in Postgres; `services/kubeletto/weekly-review.sh` section 4 prints the top five with their error share. The Ingress (Traefik) board has the edge's rates, errors and latency by route. **Per-pod disk and I/O** are not exported either: the kubelet exporter keeps only CPU, memory and network.

panels.title: Requests to tenant apps, all tenants (http)
panels.description: Requests per second reaching tenant apps through the wildcard route, by response class (stacked: the parts sum to all http requests). The 5xx here are Traefik's, mostly 504 (the tenant app did not answer in time: a cold start or a slow app), and 499 is a client that left. See the Ingress board for the edge as a whole.
